identification.name: Nylon 12 (PA12)
identification.common_form_notes: The dominant SLS (Selective Laser Sintering) 3D printing powder — most SLS-printed nylon parts are PA12 unless otherwise specified. Also stocked as bulk rod/sheet for machining, and used for its low moisture absorption and good chemical/fuel resistance in tubing and fittings.
identification.notes: Values from a generic materials-database-style source (min value of reported min–max ranges used throughout, given as a representative figure — actual grades vary within the stated range). Absorbs less moisture than PA6, so its properties are more stable in humid service than PA6's. Source's reported ductility/elongation figure (~1.9–2.1%) was not used — it reads as implausibly low for PA12, which has a reputation for high flexibility and impact toughness, and no reliable alternate figure was found across the given sources; left null rather than propagate a likely-erroneous number. Similarly, the source's stated "Minimum Service Temperature" (90 K ≈ −183 °C) reads as a generic materials-science figure rather than a practical design limit (real-world low-temperature embrittlement for nylons typically becomes a concern far above that), so usable_temp_range is left null rather than suggest an unrealistic cryogenic rating. Glass transition converted from source's 330 K. Yield strength derived from the source's "Elastic Limit" (47 MPa) — treated as the closest per-source analog to yield strength for an unreinforced thermoplastic, not a directly-labeled "yield strength" row.

typical_usage: SLS-printed functional prototypes and end-use parts (brackets, housings, snap-fits, living hinges) needing good impact toughness and low moisture pickup; fuel lines, pneumatic tubing, and cable jacketing where chemical resistance matters. Choose over PA6 when moisture stability or SLS printability is the priority; choose PA6 (or POM) instead for higher stiffness/strength bulk-machined parts.
